title: Kāmo ’kārṣīt: “desire did it”
theme: An offering formula in which the speaker attributes past wrongs to desire, not to himself, and offers ghee to desire as a deity; its pair, 10.62, does the same with anger.

words.context: anon: «कामो मकरध्वजो» — Kāma, the god whose banner is the makara
anon: «कारयिता भवति नाहं कारयिताऽस्वतन्त्रत्वान्मनुष्याणाम्» — I do not make [it] done, for men are not independent
anon: «एष आज्यभागः» — this portion of ghee

sandhi.rule: kāmaḥ + akārṣīt → kāmo ’kārṣīt: the visarga becomes o and the initial a is elided (avagraha).
akārṣīt + namaḥ → akārṣīn namaḥ: t becomes n before n.

sandhi.type: unjoined vowels; eṣaḥ before a consonant
sandhi.rule: kārayitā eṣaḥ is printed without joining the vowels (see sandhi_exceptions); eṣaḥ + te → eṣa te: eṣaḥ drops its visarga before a consonant.

sandhi_exceptions.note: kārayitā eṣa is printed with the vowels apart, at the break between the confession and the offering formula.

morphology.note: s-aorist 3rd singular of √kṛ: ‘has done’ — the deed is past and complete.
Agent noun in -tṛ: ‘the doer’, set against kārayitā, the causative agent noun ‘the one who has [it] done’.
Agent noun from the causative kāraya-: ‘the one who causes [another] to act’.

translation.literal: Desire has done [it]; homage, homage. Desire has done [it]; desire does [it], I do not do [it]; desire is the doer, I am not the doer; desire is the one who causes [it] to be done, I am not the one who causes [it] to be done. This [offering] is for you, O Desire, for desire. Svāhā.
translation.readable: Desire did it — homage, homage. Desire did it: desire acts, not I; desire is the doer, not I; desire drives the deed, not I. This offering is yours, Desire: to Desire, svāhā.

syntax: A short salutation, then three parallel pairs of clauses, each setting desire against ‘I’ with the negation na: desire does / I do not; desire is the doer / I am not; desire has it done / I do not. The last sentence is an offering formula: eṣa te … svāhā, ‘this is for you’, with the vocative and the dative of the deity.

ambiguities.note: The text names no deed; the anonymous commentator supplies ‘the sins mentioned before’: «पूर्वोक्तानि पापानि».

Read literally, the speaker says he is not the doer. The commentator discusses this directly (see commentary): the guilt lies with the one who compels, not with an unwilling doer, and the formula is spoken in remorse.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A prose formula (yajus). The salutation counts 8 syllables, the rest 44.

beginner: This is a short offering formula. The speaker says that desire did the wrong — not he himself. Desire acted, desire was the doer, desire made him do it; then he offers a spoonful of ghee into the fire to Desire, honoured as a deity, with the word svāhā. The next anuvāka repeats the same words for anger. The old commentator does not read this as an excuse. He says it is spoken by someone in remorse, who feels pushed by desire and anger into acts he did not want, and asks the deity to take the wrong away. The edition reports that reading and makes no claim about what the rite achieves.
analogy: Like someone who, looking back on an outburst, says “that was my temper talking”, and wants to be rid of the temper rather than to escape the blame.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It salutes, then three times sets desire against ‘I’: desire does, is the doer, has [it] done; I do not, am not, have not. It ends by offering ‘this’ to Desire with svāhā.

commentary.q: Whom does the speaker salute, and what is offered?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator takes the salutation as addressed to all the gods, «हे त्रयस्त्रिंशत्कोटिदेवता युष्मभ्यं नमो नमः», and the deed as the sins already named: «पूर्वोक्तानि पापानि कामो मकरध्वजोऽकार्षीच्चकार». The repetition removes the speaker’s own agency, «स्वकर्तृ[त्व]निवृत्तिः» in his words as printed, and the reason given is that desire masters the world: «काम एव कर्ता नाहं कर्ता». The offering is ghee to remove that sin: «तत्पापनिवृत्त्यर्थं ते तुभ्यमेष आज्यभागः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The commentator answers this under the next formula (10.62): guilt belongs to the one who compels, not to an unwilling doer, and the formulas are spoken by someone weeping in remorse. See 10.62.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta school commentary on this formula is in the edition’s sources: the anonymous bhāṣya reads it as a ritual formula of remorse, and neither Sāyaṇa nor Bhāskara comments on it in the copies used (their 64-anuvāka texts do not include it). Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary is not in the sources. No school position is given.

parallels.quote: अथ केन प्रयुक्तोऽयं पापं चरति पूरुषः
parallels.note: Arjuna asks what drives a person to wrong ‘even unwilling, as if by force’ — the situation the anonymous commentator describes for this formula.
The Gītā’s answer names the same two forces as the paired formulas 10.61–10.62: desire and anger.

contemporary.text: The formula separates the self from an impulse it does not endorse: “desire did it, not I.” Read with the commentator, it is not an alibi but a way of naming the impulse so that it can be given up. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: When desire pushes you into something, do you experience it as “me” or as something acting on you?
reflect.deeper: The commentator says the guilt lies with the one who compels, not the unwilling doer, yet the speaker still makes an offering. What does that combination say about responsibility?
reflect.practice: Next time desire rises, name it silently (“this is desire”) before you act.

references.text: Only the anonymous bhāṣya of the Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa comments on this anuvāka in the edition’s sources; no comment is found in Sāyaṇa’s or Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s copies.

flags.note: Whether the formula disclaims responsibility is a question of reading; the commentator’s view (guilt lies with the compeller; the formula is spoken in remorse) is reported, not adopted.

The Tirupati e-text prints an extra svāhā at the end of 10.60 and writes ष as श in कामोऽकार्षीत्; it also repeats the formula. The base and the Ānandāśrama text agree; the differences are listed on the sources page.
